book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King

chapters.file: ch02 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy.md
ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md
ch07 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction, framed as an in-game quest log ('Read a Philosophy Book,' reward: +21 Intellect), argues that WoW is a profound cultural phenomenon that deserves philosophy because the world is virtual but the people, guilds, and Blizzard developers behind it are real. It models philosophizing on Socrates' claim that he knew he did not know, inviting readers to honestly examine the guiding principles they already rely on when playing and living. Chapters can be tackled in any order like a quest log, and the goal is a more open mind about gamer life rather than final answers.

Monica Evans opens with the 2006 'Serenity Now' funeral raid — a PvP guild massacring an in-game funeral for a real player — to argue that in-game ethics depend on each player's perception of the gameworld: mourners treat Azeroth as an extension of real life, raiders as a competitive game, and both are right. Plato's Ring of Gyges fails as an analogy because WoW hands everyone invisibility, yet morality still operates as a social construction through reputation, guilds, and the ostracism of ninja-looters. She finds the Borean Tundra 'torture quest' ethically hollow since the prisoner respawns and nothing persists, applies Mill's utilitarianism to good-samaritan players and universally loathed ninja-looters, and uses Kant's Categorical Imperative both to explain why players don't desert dungeon parties and why fair PvP killing of friends is permissible.

A short story reprinted from The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction: the troll queen Willhelmia, a dungeon boss, is audited by an IRS agent who rules that the loot she hoards from heroes is taxable commission income, complete with capital gains, interest, and penalties. The comedy comes from applying real-world categories — employee, income, property, jurisdiction — to a purely virtual existence, and it ends with the IRS 'outsourcing' her debt collection, a wink at real privatized tax-collection headlines.

chapters.file: ch11 - Buffing Our Economic Knowledge with World of Warcraft.md
chapters.relation: Eli Kosminsky argues that Blizzard, probably unintentionally, built a perfectly competitive market: the auction house satisfies the textbook conditions of innumerable sellers (everyone dumping Mithril bars), homogeneous goods (every piece of Spellweave identical), perfect communication (instantly visible prices, no opportunity cost), and no barriers to entry (switching from farming Crystallized Shadows to Crystallized Fire costs nothing). He then tests the theory against server data — prices on high-population servers are nearly twice as stable as on low-population ones, and lesser and greater planar essences trade at almost exactly the predicted 3:1 ratio. Adam Smith's invisible hand works in Azeroth, making WoW a laboratory for economics that no real market could match.

Luke Cuddy asks whether playing WoW can answer nihilism, using Schopenhauer's bleak remark on our sudden existence and Nietzsche's death of God to set up the problem — King Bangalash dies and WoW goes on, just as humans die and the universe continues. Entering Huizinga's Magic Circle gives Azeroth its meanings, but the player must then dissolve the circle, recognize that the game itself is meaningless, and keep playing anyway — creating the toon as a work of art in the Dionysian spirit. A maxed Death Knight still is not Nietzsche's Overman, because the player affirms only her in-game existence; the fifth step is carrying that self-creation back into real life.

chapters.file: ch13 - Which World Am I In.md
chapters.relation: Juan Ferret tells the story from inside the game: Admetus the Human Mage, chased through Alterac Valley by an Undead Rogue, works through Zeno's paradox of motion, the convergence of infinite series, and whether space and time are discrete, coached by a bodiless voice that turns out to be his player. The voice's revelations — 'You are my creation,' autorun, polymorph, Blink — force the free-will-versus-determinism question from the character's side, since every action is controlled from above. Reference frames, Heisenberg's uncertainty, EPR entanglement, and hidden nods to David Lewis ('Siwel Divad' on possible worlds) and many-worlds theory leave the mage wondering which world, server, or parallel universe he really inhabits.

Silcox and Cogburn test Nozick's three reasons for refusing the experience machine against Azeroth. Respawning kobolds and endlessly repeated quests threaten Nozick's 'we want to do things' objection — yet play genuinely changes other players and their characters, which is what the massive multiplayer element adds over a solo machine. Attribute scores let a dullard play a genius, but as with the wheelchair-bound woman who played Doom to 'get my legs back,' piloting a warrior is still something you do, like a pilot flying a plane. Against Nozick's 'man-made reality' complaint they argue that WoW, like great art, stays open to unbounded interpretation and even surprises its own designers, so the human appetite for fun is more robust and complicated than Nozick allowed.

Paul Brown argues that Warcraft II begins by saving the player from boredom and ends by offering something like eternal happiness. Kierkegaard's 'rotation of crops' from Either/Or explains why Medivh and the Orcs grow bored into war and how console play relieves the living room's intellectual dead zone, with Heidegger supplying the definition of boredom; Nietzsche's will to power accounts both for the player's overt domination of peasants and sheep ('Stop that persistent clicking') and for the sublimated, ascetic self-overcoming of mastering the game, which Maslow redescribes as growth-needs and peak experiences. Kierkegaard's third, religious existence stage — subjective faith giving 'eternal happiness' — is playfully applied to becoming 'contemporary' with the game itself.

chapters.file: ch17 - FIVE, Dying Linking to Transcendence.md
chapters.relation: Dario Compagnio and Patrick Coppock organize WoW's collecting through Danet and Katriel's five root metaphors: hunting and gathering (quest chains as time markers), hoarding (XP and gold farming as accumulation bordering on compulsion), mating and desire (bower-bird avatar display seeking others' recognition), nurturing (group play as therapy and shared memory), and dying — collecting as linking to transcendence. The final metaphor is developed through Heidegger's being-toward-death: the endgame, like death, gives sense to all the play that precedes it, even though the hunt is never-ending. Wittgenstein's 'seeing-as' frames the whole analysis: collectibles become experientially real because players habitually perceive them as valuable, to the point of buying them on eBay.

Miguel Sicart reads the 'Gnome Tea Party' — dozens of nearly nude gnome warriors parading in Ironforge to protest Warrior-class nerfs until Blizzard banned their accounts — as non-violent protest in the tradition of Thoreau and Gandhi. Against Blizzard's models of players-as-consumers and players-as-troublemakers, which he traces to Huizinga's Homo Ludens, he argues that players are Homo poieticus: creative beings who make the values they play by and act on them. Using the 'Flourishing Ethics' framework built from Aristotle's virtue ethics and Wiener's information ethics, he concludes that WoW's architectures of control and account-banning are an unethical design that damages players' capacity to flourish — Azeroth is our world too.

chapters.file: ch20 - Embrace the Shadow!—There Is No Moral Dilemma.md
chapters.relation: Phil Serchuk asks whether ninja looters — say, a raid leader Master-Looting the Warglaive of Azzinoth — act immorally, and answers no. After reviewing act and rule utilitarianism through Medivh's opening of the Dark Portal and the theft of Napoleon's sarcophagus, and Kant's Categorical Imperative through Kil'jaeden's deception of Ner'zhul, he argues that virtual items cannot be owned at all and that there is no moral agent in WoW for either theory to condemn: neither the player (who kills thousands of PCs in battlegrounds without blame) nor the avatar (which makes no decisions) can be held liable. Ninjaing is therefore as morally benign as a natural disaster.

chapters.file: ch21 - L2Design, n00b Knowledge As Design.md
chapters.relation: Sean Duncan follows a Rogue-class forum thread — Dismalstrike's detailed redesign proposals, debated by other players and acknowledged by a rare Blizzard 'blue post' — to argue that everyday players act as informal designers co-constructing knowledge about the game. Drawing on Donald Schön's reflection-in-action, itself rooted in the pragmatism of Dewey, James, and Peirce, he rejects the idea that rational facts come first and practice second: knowing how to fix the Rogue class is built through playing, posting, iterating, and revising. Knowledge construction is design, and the stakes extend beyond gaming to how literacy, learning, and civic participation should be understood in a world where play and work blur.

Debra Jackson argues that despite its ethnic and gender stereotypes the Warcraft universe is structurally a Rawlsian liberal utopia: designers choose class balance behind a veil of ignorance, racial traits are symmetric, professions are open to all, and a difference principle guarantees even the most disadvantaged player a decent experience. Plato's Republic supplies the gender argument — as Plato made the soul rather than reproductive function the criterion for guardians, WoW makes gender irrelevant to gameplay. Yet players import real-world prejudice (anti-Gnome hate speech, female toons shunted into healer roles, mocked male Blood Elves), so structural equality never yields substantial equality: WoW is sexist and racist because we are.

Pauline Chan, Audrey Whitman, and Allan Baumer, with interleaved fiction about the warlock Reshka, analyze WoW role play as Goffmanesque social performance: three spheres of conduct (real-world codes, game mechanics, in-world lore) constrain the avatar as an 'other I' that lets players perform a 'right face' they cannot achieve offline. Factional aesthetics — Stormwind at daybreak, Orgrimmar at sunset — shape Horde and Alliance identities, and even buffing rituals become the emergent stage on which narratives like Reshka's exile from her guild play out.

chapters.file: ch25 - Epilogue Girl, You’ll Be a (Whoa ) Man Soon.md
chapters.relation: Phill Alexander recounts playing the female blood elf 'Sasha' so convincingly that his guild assumed he was a woman — and that he and his girlfriend's toon were a lesbian couple — testing Lisa Nakamura's 'identity tourism' thesis that avatars are consequence-free prostheses; months of accumulated intimacy and the ethical crisis of correcting (or concealing) the misunderstanding prove there were very real consequences. Baudrillard's simulacra and the hyperreal explain how Sasha became a signifying machine as 'real' as any guildmate, and James Gee's projective identity frames the decision to recustomize Sasha into Soren — a 'WoW witness relocation' that ends the deception without destroying the community.

chapters.file: ch26 - You Can Discover More about a Person in an Hour of Play than in a Year of.md
chapters.relation: Tim Christopher weighs pseudonymity — multiple persistent in-game identities — against responsibility for what those identities do, opening with his accidental first 'honorable kill' and the real-world extremes of a stabbing over loud WoW and a murder over a borrowed virtual sword. Using the Tae Kwon Do mat as a model of the sacred gamespace, he argues that WoW's persistent world and anonymity invite misbehavior, yet since no one is kind in WoW out of fear of punishment, any kindness there may be kindness for its own sake — an honest character may be a better person than an honest player. Plato's Allegory of the Cave is his master image: players see only shadows (avatars) of the real people behind them and must remember the world outside the cave.

chapters.file: ch28 - The Bronze Dragonflight Invisible Leadership.md
chapters.relation: Moses Wolfenstein applies The Prince to guild leadership: the infamous Dives Onyxia wipe ('50 DKP minus!') shows why being feared beats being loved — players flooded to join and even requested his abusive raid calls — so long as fear never curdles into hatred, while PUGs and battlegrounds replay Machiavelli's warning that mercenary troops are 'disunited, ambitious, without discipline, disloyal.' Against this he sets Laozi's Daodejing verse 17, where the best rulers are scarcely known by their subjects and the people credit themselves — embodied by the hidden bronze dragonflight and Chromie, and by the back-channel guild officer who invisibly paves the road to victory.

chapters.file: ch29 - What Is It Good For.md
chapters.relation: Ben Medler argues that despite the faction rhetoric there is no war in WoW. Working through definitions from Clausewitz, Rousseau (war is a relation between State and State, not man and man), and just-war thinkers like Cicero and Grotius, he shows that duelers, battleground teams, world PvP, and even guilds all lack war's defining features — political community, anonymity of victims, territorial stakes — so the fighting is feuding and gladiatorial combat, not war. Players live like egalitarian nomadic band societies, guilds are at most chiefdoms, and Blizzard alone is the state (indeed a plutocracy) that cannot war with itself; he closes by asking designers for neutral, nonviolent gameplay.

Christian Hoffstadt and Michael Nagenborg read WoW's surveillance apparatus — the Warden client scanning players' machines, EULA clauses allowing remote patching, invisible Gamemasters — through Bentham's Panopticon as analyzed by Foucault: because players can never know whether they are watched, they discipline themselves against bots and gold farming. Against Richard Bartle's claim that developers are gods rather than governments, they use Foucault's governmentality and the fragile Machiavellian prince to show that Blizzard's sovereignty must be constantly maintained against hackers, cheaters, and black markets. Surveillance is Janus-faced, though: DKP add-ons and guild self-monitoring also coordinate raiding fairly — in this panopticon the inmates can be guards too.

chapters.file: ch32 - Too Big a Byte to Chew.md
chapters.relation: Kylie Prymus uses a slain Orc to stage the metaphysics of Azeroth: whether the 'dead' Orc is anything more than electrons obeying code (Democritus's atomism), and why explaining Ironforge's empty Tuesday mornings forces us to 'go meta' just as Aristotle's Metaphysics went beyond his Physics. The problem of other minds gets a WoW twist: without nameplates we would sort NPC from PC by the argument from analogy, the same imperfect tool we use offline for pain, coma patients, and animal minds. David Lewis's plurality of worlds becomes concrete through servers — 'the gates could be open' is true for the Uther player because on Medivh they opened on January 23rd — and she concludes that the real world is no better defined than Azeroth.

Leon Spencer and Anna Janssen re-read Azeroth not as a medieval fantasy but as the surface of a post-Singularity society: magic is Clarke's 'sufficiently advanced technology' as ubiquitous computing (mana a self-recharging hydrogen fuel cell), the Titans are the AI engineers who passed through the Singularity, the Exodar a crashed colony ship measurable on Kardashev's scale, and Cure Disease and Resurrect post-scarcity medicine. The puzzle is why a post-singular people still fight endless wars over gold in a world without scarcity, and the Orwellian answer is that the Titans engineered perpetual, shifting warfare as entertainment — a stagnation that warns us to choose differently as our own Singularity approaches.

chapters.file: ch34 - I Can’t Understand True Contradictions. Try it Again . . . In Orcish.md
chapters.relation: Nicolas Michaud asks how far a gameworld can bend the rules that structure reality: mana regenerating from nowhere seems to violate conservation of energy, alternative axiom systems might license 10 + 10 = 40 damage, and sorites cases like 'balding' and Half-Elves strain the Law of Excluded Middle. The deepest case is the Law of Non-Contradiction: a true contradiction would trivialize every belief ('explosion'), and Graham Priest's 'Sylvan's Box' — a box containing something and nothing — shows we can tell a contradiction story without absurdity yet still cannot really understand it. His conclusion: WoW's designers could probably program a dialetheia, but comprehending it would require a whole different way of thinking that humans probably lack.

chapters.file: ch37 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy.md

holes.name: The Magic Circle
holes.what: Huizinga's notion (developed by Salen and Zimmerman) that accepting a game's rules encloses a bounded space where special meanings hold absolutely.
holes.why: Chapter 12's five-step escape from nihilism turns on the player entering WoW's magic circle and then dissolving it.

holes.name: Johan Huizinga
holes.what: Dutch historian whose Homo Ludens defines play as a free, separate, rule-bound activity that generates culture.
holes.why: Chapter 19 traces Blizzard's consumer and troublemaker player models to Huizinga's Homo Ludens and opposes it with Homo poieticus.

holes.name: Donald Schön
holes.what: Design theorist whose 'reflection-in-action' holds that knowledge is generated in doing, iterating, and revising rather than applied from prior rational foundations.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Schön's reflective practitioner to read WoW class forums as genuine design practice where players co-construct knowledge.

holes.name: Erving Goffman
holes.what: Sociologist of the 'presentation of self' who analyzed everyday interaction as performance managed to keep one's 'face'.
holes.why: Chapter 24 builds its account of WoW role play as cathartic social performance directly on Goffman's performance and face-work concepts.

holes.name: Identity Tourism
holes.what: Lisa Nakamura's term for donning other-gender or other-race online personae as amusing prostheses supposedly without real-life consequences.
holes.why: Chapter 25 tests identity tourism through the author's months playing a female blood elf whom his guild took for a real woman.

holes.name: The Technological Singularity
holes.what: The hypothesized point at which artificial intelligence exceeds human intelligence and self-improves beyond prediction or control.
holes.why: Chapter 33 reads all of Azeroth — its magic, gods, and perpetual war — as the remains of a society already past the Singularity.

holes.name: Dialetheism (True Contradictions)
holes.what: Graham Priest's thesis that some contradictions are really true, rejecting the Law of Non-Contradiction.
holes.why: Chapter 34 asks whether WoW's designers could program a true contradiction and tests it with Priest's 'Sylvan's Box'.
